nodes.name: Function space $\mathcal{A}_O$
nodes.statement: Further let $\mathcal{A}_O$ be a function space over $K$ possessing an $O$-module structure.

nodes.name: Model (behavior)
nodes.statement: A \textbf{model} or a so-called \textbf{behavior} $\mathcal{B}$ is the solution set of a homogeneous linear system, given by finitely many equations. These equations are defined in terms of the operator algebra $O$.
nodes.genus: solution set of a homogeneous linear system

nodes.name: Kernel representation $\mathcal{B}=\mathrm{Sol}(O^{1\times r}R)$ and action $\bullet$
nodes.statement: Thus $\mathcal{B}$ is characterized by $$ \mathcal{B}=\mathrm{Sol}(O^{1\times r}R)= \lbrace \omega \in \mathcal{A}_O^m \, | \, R \bullet \omega= 0 \rbrace, \;\;\; \mbox{ where } \; R\in O^{r \times m}$$ and $\bullet$ denotes the natural extension of the module action $o \bullet \omega$ of $o \in O$ on $\omega \in \mathcal{A}_O$ to the matrix $R \in O^{r \times m}$ and the vector $\omega \in \mathcal{A}_O^m$.
nodes.statement_short: A behavior is the solution set of $R\bullet\omega=0$ for an operator matrix $R$, with $\bullet$ the extended module action.

nodes.name: Linear exact modeling problem
nodes.statement: Suppose we observe a set of signals $\Omega \subseteq \mathcal{A}_O^m$. The aim is to find a model $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ in the model class such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ is unfalsified by $\Omega$, i.e. \ $\Omega \subseteq \mathcal{B}_\Omega$. \item $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ is most powerful, i.e.\ for every behavior $\mathcal{B}$ with $\Omega \subseteq \mathcal{B}$, it follows that $\mathcal{B}_\Omega \subseteq \mathcal{B}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Given observed signals $\Omega$, find a model containing $\Omega$ (unfalsified) and contained in every such model (most powerful).

nodes.name: Most powerful unfalsified model (MPUM)
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ is invariant under the action of $O$, that is, if we have for all $o \in O$ $$ \omega \in \mathcal{B} \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; o \bullet \omega \in \mathcal{B},$$ it is called \textbf{most powerful unfalsified model}, short $\mathrm{MPUM}$ of $\Omega$.
differentia: $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ is invariant under the action of $O$

nodes.name: Variant most powerful unfalsified model (VMPUM)
nodes.statement: Else, if $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ varies under $O$ it is called \textbf{variant most powerful unfalsified model}, short $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Notation $\mathcal{B}_\Omega^V$
nodes.statement: We denote the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$ by $\mathcal{B}_\Omega^V$.

nodes.name: MPUM versus VMPUM of the signal $\omega(t)=t$
nodes.statement: Consider the signal set consisting of a single signal $$\Omega= \lbrace \omega \rbrace, \;\;\; \mbox{where } \; \omega(t)=t \; \mbox{ for all } t \in \mathbb{R} .$$ \begin{enumerate} \item Let $O=\mathbb{C}[\partial]$ and $\mathcal{A}_O=\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$, where $\partial \bullet f := \frac{df}{dt}$. Using the commutative structure of the operator ring, the underlying system is invariant under differentiation: $$ R \bullet w = 0 \;\;\; \Rightarrow \;\;\; R ( \partial \bullet w ) = ( R \partial ) \bullet w = ( \partial R ) \bullet w = \partial ( R \bullet w) =0.$$ Since we are searching for a differentiation-invariant model, we obtain that besides $\omega$, also its derivative, the constant function $1$, belongs to $\mathcal{B}_{\Omega} $. Using that the model is $\mathbb{C}$-linear, we get that $$\mathcal{B}_{\Omega} = \{ w \ | \ \exists a,b \in \mathbb{C}: \forall t\in \mathbb{R} : w(t)=at+b \}.$$ An element $w \in \mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$ is contained in $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ if and only if $$\partial^2 \bullet w=0,$$ i.e. the $\mathrm{MPUM}$ is specified by a single ordinary differential equation with constant coefficients. \item Now let $O=\mathbb{C}[t]\langle \partial \rangle$, where $\partial \bullet f := \frac{df}{dt}$ and $\mathcal{A}_O$ is defined as above. We want to describe $\omega$ as a solution of homogeneous ordinary differential equations with polynomial coefficients. The equations $$\partial^2 \bullet w=0 \;\; \mbox{ and } \;\; t \partial \bullet w-w=0 $$ are satisfied by $\omega$. We will see later that these two generate a kernel representation of the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$. The corresponding solution space equals $$\mathcal{B}_\Omega^V=\{ w \ | \ \exists a \in \mathbb{C} : \forall t\in{\mathbb{R}} : w(t)=at\}.$$ Notice that this example demonstrates the variance under $\partial$, since we have $ \partial \bullet \omega \notin \mathcal{B}_\Omega^V$. Another property that should be pointed out is that the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ yields a more precise description of $\Omega$ than $\mathrm{MPUM}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $\omega(t)=t$ the MPUM over $\mathbb{C}[\partial]$ is all affine functions, while the VMPUM over $\mathbb{C}[t]\langle\partial\rangle$ is $\{at\}$.
nodes.label: MotivatingExample

nodes.name: Ore extension (skew polynomial ring) and Ore algebra
nodes.statement: \cite{MR} \ \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] Let $A$ be a ring and $\sigma : A \rightarrow A$ be a ring endomorphism. \begin{enumerate} \item The map $\delta : A \rightarrow A$ is called a $\sigma$-\textbf{derivation} if it is $K$-linear and satisfies the skew Leibniz rule \begin{align} \delta(a b) = \sigma(a) \delta(b) + \delta(a) b \;\;\;\; \mbox{for all } a, b \in A. \end{align} \item For a $\sigma$-derivation $\delta$, the ring $A\left[ \partial;\sigma, \delta \right] $ which consists of all polynomials in $\partial$ with coefficients in $A$ with the usual addition and a product defined by the commutation rule $$\partial a = \sigma(a) \partial + \delta(a) \;\;\;\; \mbox{for all } a \in A,$$ is called a \textbf{skew polynomial ring} or an \textbf{Ore extension} of $A$ with $\sigma$ and $\delta$. \end{enumerate} \item[] If $A$ is a domain and $\sigma$ is injective, the skew polynomial ring $A\left[ \partial;\sigma, \delta \right]$ is a domain by degree arguments. Then the definition can be iterated to the so-called Ore algebras \cite{CS}. \item[(2)] Let $A=K[t_1, \dots, t_n]$. An iterated skew polynomial ring $$O=K[t_1, \dots, t_n] [\partial_1;\sigma_1, \delta_1] \cdots [\partial_s;\sigma_s, \delta_s]$$ is called a (polynomial) \textbf{Ore algebra} if the $\sigma_i$'s and $\delta_j$'s commute for $ 1 \leq i , j \leq s $, the $\partial_i$'s commute with $\partial_j$'s and further for all $1\leq i \leq s$ the map $\sigma_i:O \rightarrow O$ is an injective $K$-algebra endomorphism and $\delta_i:O \rightarrow O $ is a $\sigma_i$-derivation satisfying $ \sigma_i( \partial_j)= \partial_j \;\;\;\; \mbox{ and }\;\;\;\; \delta_i(\partial_j)=0. $ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Defines $\sigma$-derivations, Ore extensions $A[\partial;\sigma,\delta]$ with $\partial a=\sigma(a)\partial+\delta(a)$, and polynomial Ore algebras as commuting iterated Ore extensions of $K[t_1,\dots,t_n]$.
nodes.label: defOre

nodes.name: Skew Leibniz rule
nodes.statement: \delta(a b) = \sigma(a) \delta(b) + \delta(a) b \;\;\;\; \mbox{for all } a, b \in A.
nodes.label: deltaOperation

nodes.name: Normal form in an Ore algebra
nodes.statement: Using multi-index notation, every element of an Ore algebra can be expressed into the normal form $$ \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^s} p_\alpha \partial^\alpha = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^s} p_\alpha {\partial_1}^{\alpha_1} \cdot \ldots \cdot {\partial_s}^{\alpha_s} \;\;\;\; \mbox{ where } \;\; p_\alpha \in A. $$
assumptions: Using multi-index notation
conclusions: every element of an Ore algebra can be expressed into the normal form

nodes.name: Weyl, difference, SW and q-difference algebras
nodes.statement: Let $n=1$, thus $A=K[t]$. The algebras can be iterated to $n \in \mathbb{N}$. \begin{enumerate} \item The first \textbf{Weyl algebra} is defined by $\mathrm{W}_1:= A[ \partial; \mathrm{id}_{ \mathrm{W}_1}, \frac{\partial}{\partial t}]$ with the commutation rule $ \partial t = t \partial + 1 .$ \item The first \textbf{difference algebra} is defined by $ \mathcal{S}_1 :=A \left[ \Delta; \sigma, \delta \right]$, where $ (\sigma p)(t) = p(t + 1)$ and $\delta(p)=\sigma(p)-p$ for all $p \in \mathcal{S}_1$. The commutation rule is $ \Delta t = t \Delta + \Delta + 1.$ \item The following Ore algebra is a combination of the first and second one. Define $\mathcal{SW}_1:=A \left[ \Delta; \sigma_1, \delta_1 \right]\left[ \partial; \sigma_2, \delta_2 \right]$, where $\sigma_2:=id_{ \mathcal{SW}_1 }$, $\delta_2:=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}$ and $ (\sigma_1 p)(t) = p(t + 1)$, $\delta_1(p)=\sigma_1(p)-p$ for all $p \in \mathcal{SW}_1$. Then $ \partial t = t \partial + 1$, $\Delta t = t \Delta + \Delta +1$ and $\partial \Delta = \Delta \partial$. \item Suppose $q$ to be a parameter. The first \textbf{continuous $q$-difference algebra} is defined by $ \mathcal{Q}:= A [\partial; \sigma, \delta], $ where $\sigma( p )=p(q t)$ and $\delta(p)= p(qt)-p(t)$. We obtain the commutation rule $ \partial t = qt \partial + (q-1)t$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Defines the first Weyl algebra, difference algebra, mixed difference-differential algebra $\mathcal{SW}_1$ and continuous $q$-difference algebra with their commutation rules.
nodes.label: interestingAlgebras

nodes.name: Shifted Ore extension isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a ring, and $A[\partial; \sigma,\delta]$ be an Ore extension of $A$. For any $\alpha \in A$ there exists an Ore extension $A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta']$ with $\delta'(a) = \sigma(a) \alpha - \alpha a + \delta(a)$, such that $A[\partial; \sigma,\delta] \cong A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta'] $ as rings.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a ring, and $A[\partial; \sigma,\delta]$ be an Ore extension of $A$.
For any $\alpha \in A$
conclusions: there exists an Ore extension $A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta']$ with $\delta'(a) = \sigma(a) \alpha - \alpha a + \delta(a)$, such that $A[\partial; \sigma,\delta] \cong A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta'] $ as rings.
nodes.statement_short: Replacing $\partial$ by $\partial-\alpha$ gives an isomorphic Ore extension with a modified $\sigma$-derivation.
nodes.label: OreIso

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: For all $a \in A$, the equality $\partial a = \sigma(a) \partial + \delta(a)$ holds. For $\alpha \in A$ define $\Delta_{\alpha} := \partial - \alpha$. Then it obeys the relation $\Delta_{\alpha} a = \sigma(a) \Delta_{\alpha} + \sigma(a) \alpha - \alpha a + \delta(a) = \sigma(a)\Delta_{\alpha} + \delta'(a)$. The map $\delta'$ is linear and it is a $\sigma$-derivation since \[ \delta'(ab) = \sigma(a) \sigma(b) \alpha - \sigma(a) \alpha b + \sigma(a) \delta(b) - \sigma(a) \alpha b - \alpha ab + \delta(a)b = \] \[ \sigma(a) \sigma(b) \alpha - \alpha ab + \sigma(a) \delta(b) - \delta(a)b = \sigma(ab) \alpha - \alpha ab + \delta(ab). \] Define the ring homomorphism $\varphi_{\alpha}: A[\partial; \sigma,\delta] \to A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta']$, $\varphi_{\alpha}(a)=a$ for all $a \in A$, $\varphi_{\alpha}(\partial)=\Delta_{\alpha}=\partial - \alpha$. Then $\varphi_{\alpha}$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\Delta_\alpha=\partial-\alpha$, verify the new commutation rule and that $\delta'$ is a $\sigma$-derivation, then the substitution map is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Introduce $\Delta_\alpha$
nodes.statement: For all $a \in A$, the equality $\partial a = \sigma(a) \partial + \delta(a)$ holds. For $\alpha \in A$ define $\Delta_{\alpha} := \partial - \alpha$. Then it obeys the relation $\Delta_{\alpha} a = \sigma(a) \Delta_{\alpha} + \sigma(a) \alpha - \alpha a + \delta(a) = \sigma(a)\Delta_{\alpha} + \delta'(a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Delta_\alpha=\partial-\alpha$ and derive its commutation rule with $\delta'$.

nodes.name: Check $\delta'$ is a $\sigma$-derivation
nodes.statement: The map $\delta'$ is linear and it is a $\sigma$-derivation since \[ \delta'(ab) = \sigma(a) \sigma(b) \alpha - \sigma(a) \alpha b + \sigma(a) \delta(b) - \sigma(a) \alpha b - \alpha ab + \delta(a)b = \] \[ \sigma(a) \sigma(b) \alpha - \alpha ab + \sigma(a) \delta(b) - \delta(a)b = \sigma(ab) \alpha - \alpha ab + \delta(ab). \]
nodes.statement_short: Verify the skew Leibniz rule for $\delta'$ by direct expansion.

nodes.name: Isomorphism $\varphi_\alpha$
nodes.statement: Define the ring homomorphism $\varphi_{\alpha}: A[\partial; \sigma,\delta] \to A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta']$, $\varphi_{\alpha}(a)=a$ for all $a \in A$, $\varphi_{\alpha}(\partial)=\Delta_{\alpha}=\partial - \alpha$. Then $\varphi_{\alpha}$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude with the substitution isomorphism $\partial\mapsto\partial-\alpha$.

nodes.name: $A$ is an $O$-module via $\partial_i\bullet p=\delta_i(p)$
nodes.statement: Let $O:= A[\partial_1; \sigma_1,\delta_1]\cdots[\partial_m; \sigma_m,\delta_m]$ be an Ore algebra. With the action $$ \partial_i \bullet p := \delta_i(p) \;\;\; \mbox{ and } \;\;\; a \bullet p :=a \cdot p \;\;\; \mbox{ for all } p\in A \mbox{ and } a \in A $$ the $K$-algebra $A$ becomes an $O$-module.
assumptions: Let $O:= A[\partial_1; \sigma_1,\delta_1]\cdots[\partial_m; \sigma_m,\delta_m]$ be an Ore algebra.
conclusions: the $K$-algebra $A$ becomes an $O$-module.

nodes.name: Proof that $A$ is an $O$-module
nodes.statement: For this, we have to show that \begin{enumerate} \item $ (o_1 \cdot o_2) \bullet p = o_1 \bullet ( o_2 \bullet p ) \;\;\;\; $ for all $o_1, o_2 \in O$ and $p \in A$ \item $ (o_1 + o_2) \bullet p = o_1 \bullet p + o_2 \bullet p \;\;\;\; $ for all $o_1, o_2 \in O$ and $p \in A$ \item $ o \bullet (p+q) = o \bullet p + o \bullet q \;\;\;\; $ for all $o \in O$ and $p, q \in A.$ \end{enumerate} To show 1. it suffices to consider $o_1=a \partial_i$ and $o_2= b \partial_j$ with $a, b \in A$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} (o_1 \cdot o_2) \bullet p & = & (\, a( \, \sigma_i(b) \partial_i + \delta_i(b)\,) \partial_j \,) \bullet p = (\, a\sigma_i(b) \partial_i \partial_j + a\delta_i(b) \partial_j \,) \bullet p \\ & = & a\sigma_i(b) \delta_i(p) \delta_j(p) + a\delta_i(b) \delta_j(p) = a \, \delta_i (b\delta_j(p)) = a \partial_i \bullet (\, b \partial_j \bullet p \,)\\ & = & o_1 \bullet (\, o_2 \bullet p \,). \end{eqnarray*} The equality in 2. and 3. holds by similar arguments.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the module axioms; associativity is checked on monomials $a\partial_i$, $b\partial_j$ by expansion, the rest similarly.

nodes.name: Module axioms to verify
nodes.statement: For this, we have to show that \begin{enumerate} \item $ (o_1 \cdot o_2) \bullet p = o_1 \bullet ( o_2 \bullet p ) \;\;\;\; $ for all $o_1, o_2 \in O$ and $p \in A$ \item $ (o_1 + o_2) \bullet p = o_1 \bullet p + o_2 \bullet p \;\;\;\; $ for all $o_1, o_2 \in O$ and $p \in A$ \item $ o \bullet (p+q) = o \bullet p + o \bullet q \;\;\;\; $ for all $o \in O$ and $p, q \in A.$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: List the three module axioms to check.

nodes.name: Verify associativity on monomials
nodes.statement: To show 1. it suffices to consider $o_1=a \partial_i$ and $o_2= b \partial_j$ with $a, b \in A$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} (o_1 \cdot o_2) \bullet p & = & (\, a( \, \sigma_i(b) \partial_i + \delta_i(b)\,) \partial_j \,) \bullet p = (\, a\sigma_i(b) \partial_i \partial_j + a\delta_i(b) \partial_j \,) \bullet p \\ & = & a\sigma_i(b) \delta_i(p) \delta_j(p) + a\delta_i(b) \delta_j(p) = a \, \delta_i (b\delta_j(p)) = a \partial_i \bullet (\, b \partial_j \bullet p \,)\\ & = & o_1 \bullet (\, o_2 \bullet p \,). \end{eqnarray*} The equality in 2. and 3. holds by similar arguments.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to monomials and expand; the other axioms follow similarly.

nodes.name: Kernel $\ker_A f$ of an operator
nodes.statement: Using this action, we can define the kernel of a linear operator $f$ from the Ore algebra $O$ over a ring $A$ to be $\ker_{A} f := \{ a\in A \mid f \bullet a = 0\}$, which is a $K$-vector space.

nodes.name: Operators with zero derivation part
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field, $A$ be a $K$-algebra, $\partial$ be a $K$-linear operator, acting on $A$ and $B = A[\partial; \sigma, \delta]$ be the corresponding operator algebra (that is, for all $a \in A$ we have $ \partial a = \sigma(a) \partial + \delta(a)$). Then the following holds: (i) $\ker_A \partial = A \Leftrightarrow \delta = 0 \Leftrightarrow B = A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$. (ii) If $\ker_A \partial = A$, then we have for $\Delta := \partial - 1$: $A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$ is isomorphic as $K$-algebra to operator algebra $A[\Delta; \sigma, \delta']$ with $\delta' := \sigma - 1$. Moreover, $\ker_A \Delta = \{a\in A\mid \sigma(a) = a\} = \mathrm{const}_{\sigma} A \subseteq A$ with the equality if and only if $A$ is invariant under $\sigma$, what is the case if $\sigma = 1_A$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a field, $A$ be a $K$-algebra, $\partial$ be a $K$-linear operator, acting on $A$ and $B = A[\partial; \sigma, \delta]$ be the corresponding operator algebra
conclusions: (i) $\ker_A \partial = A \Leftrightarrow \delta = 0 \Leftrightarrow B = A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$.
$A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$ is isomorphic as $K$-algebra to operator algebra $A[\Delta; \sigma, \delta']$ with $\delta' := \sigma - 1$.
nodes.statement_short: $\partial$ acts trivially on $A$ iff $\delta=0$; then $\Delta=\partial-1$ gives an isomorphic algebra whose kernel is the $\sigma$-constants.
nodes.label: CorDelta

nodes.name: Nontrivial operators
nodes.statement: Using Lemmata \ref{OreIso} and \ref{CorDelta}, we pass to the new setting of operators, which action $\bullet$ is nontrivial on $A$. We call such an operator nontrivial and from now on, we work with such operators only.

nodes.name: Forward shift algebra and Manin's quantum plane
nodes.statement: Consider the two most important operator algebras, built from operators having zero kernels. The first \textbf{forward shift algebra} is defined by $K[t] \left[ s; \sigma, 0 \right]$ with $(\sigma f)(t) = f(t + 1)$ for all $f \in K[t]$. The commutation rule is $s t = t s + s$. There is a natural operator associated to $s$, namely the difference operator $\Delta = s-1$, already defined in \ref{interestingAlgebras}, obeying the relation $\Delta t = t \Delta + \Delta + 1$. Applying Lemma \ref{CorDelta}, we see by degree argument, that $\ker \Delta = K$ and the two algebras are isomorphic both as Ore extensions and $K$-algebras. \\ Let $q$ be transcendental over $K$. Then the first \textbf{$q$-commutative algebra} (or Manin's quantum plane) is defined as $K_q[x,y]:=K(q)[x][\partial;\sigma,0]$ with $(\sigma f)(x)=f(qx)$ for $f\in K[t]$. Again, there is a natural $q$-difference operator $\Delta_q := \partial - 1$ and the corresponding operator algebra has been already described in \ref{interestingAlgebras} as the first continuous $q$-difference algebra. Its commutation rule reads as $\partial t = qt \partial + (q-1)t$.

nodes.name: Left submodule ${}_O\langle o_1,\dots,o_k\rangle$
nodes.statement: For $o_1, \dots, o_k \in O^{n}$, we denote by ${}_O \langle o_1, \dots o_k \rangle$ the left submodule of $O^n$, generated by $o_1, \dots, o_k$.

nodes.name: $O/{}_O\langle\partial_1,\dots,\partial_s\rangle \cong A$
nodes.statement: Let $O$ be an Ore $A$-algebra, built from operators $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_s$ which have non-zero kernels. Then there is an isomorphism of left $O$-modules $$ O/ {}_O \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle \cong A. $$
assumptions: Let $O$ be an Ore $A$-algebra, built from operators $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_s$ which have non-zero kernels.
conclusions: there is an isomorphism of left $O$-modules $$ O/ {}_O \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle \cong A. $$
nodes.label: IsoOrePoly

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement: There is a left $O$-module homomorphism $$ \varphi : O \rightarrow A, \;\;\; a=\sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^s} a_{\alpha} \partial^\alpha \mapsto a \bullet 1 $$ since $\varphi(b\cdot a) = (b\cdot a) \bullet 1= b\bullet \varphi(a)$. Due to Def. \ref{defOre} (\ref{deltaOperation}) we have $\delta(1)=0$ and thus $a \bullet 1=a_0$. The kernel of $\varphi$ is given by the left ideal ${}_{O} \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle $. Further,~$\varphi$ is clearly surjective. So the claim follows from the homomorphism theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluation at 1, $a\mapsto a\bullet 1$, is a surjective module map with kernel the left ideal of the $\partial_i$; apply the homomorphism theorem.

nodes.name: Evaluation map $\varphi$
nodes.statement: There is a left $O$-module homomorphism $$ \varphi : O \rightarrow A, \;\;\; a=\sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^s} a_{\alpha} \partial^\alpha \mapsto a \bullet 1 $$ since $\varphi(b\cdot a) = (b\cdot a) \bullet 1= b\bullet \varphi(a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the module homomorphism $a\mapsto a\bullet 1$.

nodes.name: $a\bullet 1=a_0$
nodes.statement: Due to Def. \ref{defOre} (\ref{deltaOperation}) we have $\delta(1)=0$ and thus $a \bullet 1=a_0$.
nodes.statement_short: By the skew Leibniz rule $\delta(1)=0$, so evaluation picks the constant coefficient.

nodes.name: Kernel, surjectivity, homomorphism theorem
nodes.statement: The kernel of $\varphi$ is given by the left ideal ${}_{O} \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle $. Further,~$\varphi$ is clearly surjective. So the claim follows from the homomorphism theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the kernel as the left ideal of the $\partial_i$, note surjectivity, and apply the homomorphism theorem.

nodes.name: Class $[p]$ of a polynomial
nodes.statement: Following Theorem \ref{IsoOrePoly}, every polynomial $p \in A$ can be viewed as an element of the left $O$-module $O / {}_O \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle$ by identifying $p$ with $p + {}_{O} \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle=:[p]$.

nodes.name: $\partial_i$ acts on $[p]$ as $\delta_i$
nodes.statement: Then the action of $\partial_i$ is exactly the $\sigma_i$-derivation $\delta_i$, since \begin{eqnarray*} \partial_i [p] = [ \partial_i p] = [ \sigma_i(p) \partial_i + \delta_i(p)] = [\delta_i(p)] = [\partial_i \bullet p]. \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Annihilator criterion via the left ideal of the $\partial_i$
nodes.statement: Let $p \in A$ and $o \in O$. Then there is the following equivalence \begin{eqnarray*} o \bullet p =0 \;\;\; \mbox{ if and only if } \;\;\; o \cdot p \in {}_{O} \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle. \end{eqnarray*}
assumptions: Let $p \in A$ and $o \in O$.
conclusions: o \bullet p =0 \;\;\; \mbox{ if and only if } \;\;\; o \cdot p \in {}_{O} \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle.
nodes.label: ann

nodes.name: Proof of Remark 2.8
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{IsoOrePoly}, we have an $O$-module isomorphism $A \!\cong\! O / {}_O \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle$ given by $$ A \stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} O / {}_O \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle, \;\;\;\;\; p \mapsto [p]. $$ Since the $O$-module structure is respected, $o \bullet p$ maps to $[o \cdot p]$ and hence the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Transport through the module isomorphism $A\cong O/{}_O\langle\partial\rangle$ of Theorem 2.7.

nodes.name: Map $\kappa_p$ and annihilator $\mathrm{Ann}_O(p)$
nodes.statement: Consider the map \begin{equation} \kappa_p : O \rightarrow O / {}_O\langle\partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle, \;\;\;\;\; o \mapsto o \cdot [p], \end{equation} which is clearly a left $O$-module homomorphism with the kernel $$\ker(\kappa_p) = \mathrm{Ann}_O(p):=\{ o \in O \ | \ o \bullet p=0 \}, $$ which is a left ideal in $O$.
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa_p:o\mapsto o\cdot[p]$ is a module homomorphism whose kernel is the annihilator $\mathrm{Ann}_O(p)$.

nodes.name: Definition of $\kappa_p$
nodes.statement: \kappa_p : O \rightarrow O / {}_O\langle\partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle, \;\;\;\;\; o \mapsto o \cdot [p],
nodes.label: kappa_p

nodes.name: Action of $O^{1\times m}$ on $A^m$
nodes.statement: Suppose $p= \left[ p_1, \dots, p_m \right]^{T} \in A^m$. An element of $o \in O^{1 \times m}$ naturally acts on $p$ by $$o \bullet p := \sum_{i=1}^m o_i \bullet p_i .$$

nodes.name: Invariant subset
nodes.statement: A subset $B \subseteq A^m$ is called \textbf{invariant} under $G \subseteq O^{1 \times m}$ if and only if $o \bullet p = 0$ for all $o \in G$ and $p \in B$.
differentia: $o \bullet p = 0$ for all $o \in G$ and $p \in B$

nodes.name: Vector map $\kappa_p$
nodes.statement: The set of elements under which $p$ is invariant has an $O$-module structure and equals to the kernel of $$ \kappa_p : O^{1 \times m} \rightarrow O / {}_O \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle, \;\;\;\;\; o=[o_1, \dots, o_m] \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^m o_i \cdot [p_i]. $$

nodes.name: Isomorphism $O^{1\times m}/\ker(\kappa_p)$
nodes.statement: Moreover the following isomorphism holds $$O^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong {}_{O}\langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle / {}_{O}\langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle \cap {}_{O}\langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle .$$
conclusions: $$O^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong {}_{O}\langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle / {}_{O}\langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle \cap {}_{O}\langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle .$$

nodes.name: Proof of the isomorphism for $\ker(\kappa_p)$
nodes.statement: The image of $\kappa_p$ equals $( {}_{O} \langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle + {}_{O}\langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle ) / {}_{O}\langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle.$ This is isomorphic to $ {}_{O}\langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle / {}_{O}\langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle \cap {}_{O}\langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle$. So the claim follows, since $\kappa_p$ is a homomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the image of $\kappa_p$ and apply the second isomorphism theorem.

nodes.name: Image of $\kappa_p$
nodes.statement: The image of $\kappa_p$ equals $( {}_{O} \langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle + {}_{O}\langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle ) / {}_{O}\langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle.$
nodes.statement_short: Identify the image of $\kappa_p$.

nodes.name: Second isomorphism theorem
nodes.statement: This is isomorphic to $ {}_{O}\langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle / {}_{O}\langle p_1, \dots, p_m \rangle \cap {}_{O}\langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the image by the second isomorphism theorem.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: So the claim follows, since $\kappa_p$ is a homomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by the first isomorphism theorem.

nodes.name: Finite generation of $\ker(\kappa_p)$ and $\mathrm{Ann}_O(p)$
nodes.statement: If $O$ is Noetherian (see \cite{MR}), then the left submodule $\ker(\kappa_p) \subseteq O^{1 \times m}$ is finitely generated. \\ For a polynomial $m$-tuple $p\in A^m$, we consider \[ \mathrm{Ann}_O (p) = \{ o\in O \mid o \bullet p = 0 \} = \{ o\in O \mid o \bullet p_i = 0 \ \forall \ i \} = \bigcap \mathrm{Ann}_O (p_i), \] which is a left ideal in $O$. As we see immediately, $\mathrm{Ann}_O (p)^{1\times m}$ is a (usually strict) submodule of $\ker(\kappa_p)$ and hence, the latter typically has more interesting structure, see Example \ref{exKerP}. It is always possible to recover $\mathrm{Ann}_O (p)$ from $\ker(\kappa_p)$. In our opinion, using $\ker(\kappa_p)$ is more natural in the context of vectors of signals.
nodes.label: finitely

nodes.name: Noetherian Ore algebra
nodes.statement: Let $O$ be a Noetherian Ore algebra.

nodes.name: Finitely presented module
nodes.statement: Moreover, let $M$ be a finitely presented left $O$-module, that is, there exists a matrix $P\in O^{m \times n}$ such that there is the following exact sequence of left $O$-modules: \[ O^{1\times m} \stackrel{P}{\rightarrow} O^{1 \times n} \rightarrow M \rightarrow 0. \]

nodes.name: Left syzygy module
nodes.statement: Recall that for a tuple $F= (f_1,\ldots,f_s), f_i \subset O^{1\times n}$, the set $\mathrm{LeftSyz}(F) := \{ [a_1,\ldots,a_s] \in O^{1\times s} \mid \sum_i a_i f_i = 0 \}$ carries the structure of a left $O$-module and is called the \textbf{left syzygy module} of $F$.

nodes.name: Canonical basis $\{e_i\}$
nodes.statement: Let $\{e_i \}$ be the canonical basis of the free module $O^{1\times \ell} = \overset{\ell}{\underset{i=1}{\bigoplus}} O e_i$.

nodes.name: Elimination of module components; kernel of a module homomorphism
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item \textit{``Elimination of module components''}. \\ Let $S\subset O^{1\times \ell}$ be a submodule. Moreover, let $<_O$ be a monomial ordering on $O$ and $<_m=(c,<_O)$ be a \textit{position over term} monomial module ordering on the free module $O^{1\times \ell}$, defined as follows. The components are ordered in a descending way $e_1 > \dots > e_{\ell}$ and for any monomials $o_1, o_2 \in O$ \[ o_1 e_i <_m o_2 e_j \; \Leftrightarrow \; j < i \; \text{ or } \; (j = i \text{ and } o_1 <_O o_2). \] Let $G$ be a Gr\"obner basis of $S$ with respect to $<_m$. Then $\forall \; 1\leq k < \ell \;\;$ $G \cap \overset{\ell}{\underset{i=k}{\oplus}} O e_i$ is a Gr\"obner basis of $S \cap\overset{\ell}{\underset{i=k}{\oplus}} O e_i$. \item \textit{``Kernel of a homomorphism of modules''}. \\ Consider an $O$-module homomorphism $O^{1 \times s} \stackrel{\psi}{\rightarrow} O^{1 \times n}/ O^{1\times m}P $, $e_i \mapsto [\Psi_i]$, where $\Psi_i \in O^{1 \times n}$. Let $P_i$ be the $i$-th row of the matrix $P$. Then \[ \ker \psi = \mathrm{LeftSyz}( \ (\Psi_1,\ldots,\Psi_s,P_1,\ldots,P_m) \ ) \cap \bigoplus_{i=1}^s O e_i. \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: With a position-over-term ordering, a Gröbner basis restricted to trailing components is a Gröbner basis of the eliminated module; kernels of module maps are syzygies intersected with the first components.
nodes.label: EliOfCom

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Define $W= \overset{\ell}{\underset{i=k}{\bigoplus}} O e_i$. Since $G$ is a Gr\"obner basis of $S$, for any $s \in S$ there exists $g \in G$ such that $\mathrm{lm}(g)$ divides $\mathrm{lm}(s)$. If $s\in S \cap W$, then $\mathrm{lm}(g) \in W$ and hence, by definition of $<_m$, we have $g \in W$ and $g \in G \cap W$. So, $G \cap W$ is a Gr\"obner basis of $S\cap W$. \item We have \[ [b_1,\ldots,b_s] \in \ker \psi \ \Leftrightarrow \ \exists a_k\in O \ : \ \sum_{i=1}^s b_i \Psi_i + \sum_{k=1}^m a_k P_k =0 \ \Leftrightarrow \] \[ [b_1,\ldots,b_s] \in \mathrm{LeftSyz}(\ (\Psi_1,\ldots,\Psi_s,P_1,\ldots,P_m)\ ) \cap \bigoplus_{i=1}^s O e_i. \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: (1) Leading monomials of elements of the trailing components lie there by the ordering; (2) unfold the definition of the kernel into a syzygy condition.

nodes.name: Part 1: elimination
nodes.statement: Define $W= \overset{\ell}{\underset{i=k}{\bigoplus}} O e_i$. Since $G$ is a Gr\"obner basis of $S$, for any $s \in S$ there exists $g \in G$ such that $\mathrm{lm}(g)$ divides $\mathrm{lm}(s)$. If $s\in S \cap W$, then $\mathrm{lm}(g) \in W$ and hence, by definition of $<_m$, we have $g \in W$ and $g \in G \cap W$. So, $G \cap W$ is a Gr\"obner basis of $S\cap W$.
nodes.statement_short: The position-over-term ordering forces divisors of leading monomials in $W$ to lie in $W$.

nodes.name: Part 2: kernel via syzygies
nodes.statement: We have \[ [b_1,\ldots,b_s] \in \ker \psi \ \Leftrightarrow \ \exists a_k\in O \ : \ \sum_{i=1}^s b_i \Psi_i + \sum_{k=1}^m a_k P_k =0 \ \Leftrightarrow \] \[ [b_1,\ldots,b_s] \in \mathrm{LeftSyz}(\ (\Psi_1,\ldots,\Psi_s,P_1,\ldots,P_m)\ ) \cap \bigoplus_{i=1}^s O e_i. \]
nodes.statement_short: Membership in $\ker\psi$ is exactly a syzygy condition restricted to the first $s$ components.

nodes.name: Annihilator of a module element; intersection of submodules
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item \textit{``Annihilator of an element in a module''}. \\ Let $M = O^{1 \times n}/O^{1\times m}P$ and let $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ be the rows of $P$. Moreover, let $v \in O^{1\times n}$. Then the left ideal $\mathrm{Ann}_M^{O} (v) := \{ a\in O \mid a[v] = 0 \in M\}\subseteq O$ can be computed as \[ \mathrm{Ann}_M^{O} (v) = \ker (O \stackrel{\cdot [v]}{\rightarrow} M) = \mathrm{LeftSyz}(\ (v,P_1,\ldots,P_m)\ ) \cap O e_1. \] \item \textit{"Intersection of finitely many submodules''}. \\ Let $N_1, \ldots, N_m \subset O^{1\times r}$ be submodules. Then \[ \bigcap_{i=1}^m N_i = \ker \bigl( O^{1\times r} \rightarrow (O^{1\times r} / N_1) \oplus \cdots \oplus (O^{1\times r} / N_m), \;\; e_i \mapsto ([e_i],\ldots,[e_i]) \bigr). \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Annihilators of module elements and intersections of submodules are computable as kernels of module homomorphisms via syzygies.
nodes.label: corBasics

nodes.name: Kernels of maps between finitely presented modules and implementation
nodes.statement: For an $O$-module homomorphism $O^{1 \times s}/O^{1\times r}Q \!\stackrel{\psi'}{\rightarrow} \! O^{1 \times n}/O^{1\times m}P$, its kernel is the image of $\ker \psi$ (as in Theorem~\ref{propBasics}) under the natural projection $O^{1 \times s} \rightarrow O^{1 \times s}/ O^{1\times r}Q$. A left Gr\"obner basis can be obtained by reducing a left Gr\"obner basis of $\ker \psi + O^{1\times r}Q$ with a left Gr\"obner basis of $O^{1\times r}Q$, see \cite{LV05}.\\ Note that in practical computations, elimination of module components is usually not complicated. This stands in distinct contrast with the elimination of algebra variables, which is often very hard to achieve. The algorithms used in this article involve only the elimination of module components and thus are feasible in practice.\\ The algorithms we have discussed are implemented in computer algebra systems like e.g. \textsc{Singular::Plural} \cite{Plural} or {\sc Maple} \cite{CQR, CS} with the package \textsc{OreModules}. More background on these algorithms can be found in e.g. \cite{Kr}, \cite{LV05}. \\ In particular, a set of generators of $\ker(\kappa_p)$ from the previous section can be calculated explicitly. By Proposition \ref{EliOfCom}(2) $\ker(\kappa_p)$ is obtained via the kernel of a module homomorphism, that is, by one Gr\"obner basis computation with respect to module monomial ordering eliminating components. The monomial part of this ordering can be chosen arbitrarily to be e.~g.~a fast one.

nodes.name: Noetherian Ore algebra acting nontrivially
nodes.statement: Suppose $O$ to be a Noetherian Ore algebra with the additional property that $\partial_i$ acts nontrivially on $A$ for all $1 \leq i \leq s $.

nodes.name: $A \subseteq \mathcal{A}_O$
nodes.statement: Suppose further that $A \subseteq \mathcal{A}_O$.

nodes.name: Noetherianity of Ore extensions
nodes.statement: $[$ \cite{MR}, Theorem 1.2.9.$]$ Since $A$ is Noetherian, $O$ is Noetherian if $\sigma_i$ is an automorphism for all $1\leq i\leq s$ on $A$.
assumptions: Since $A$ is Noetherian
$\sigma_i$ is an automorphism for all $1\leq i\leq s$ on $A$
conclusions: $O$ is Noetherian
nodes.label: noetherian

nodes.name: The Ore algebras of Example 2.2 are Noetherian
nodes.statement: Thus all Ore algebras considered in Example \ref{interestingAlgebras} are Noetherian.

nodes.name: Nontrivial action makes the model vary
nodes.statement: Suppose that the $\sigma$-derivation acts nontrivially on $A$. Then the corresponding most powerful unfalsified model varies under $O$.
assumptions: Suppose that the $\sigma$-derivation acts nontrivially on $A$.
conclusions: the corresponding most powerful unfalsified model varies under $O$.

nodes.name: VMPUM of a single polynomial signal
nodes.statement: Let $p\in A^m$ be given. Consider the map $\kappa_p$ from (\ref{kappa_p}). Let $\ker(\kappa_p)={}_{O} \langle k_1, \dots, k_r \rangle$ and let $R \in O^{r \times m}$ be a matrix whose $i$-th row equals $k_i$. Then the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $ \lbrace p \rbrace$ is given by $$ \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V= \left\lbrace g\in \mathcal{A}_O^m \; | \; R \bullet g=0 \right\rbrace. $$
assumptions: Let $p\in A^m$ be given.
Let $\ker(\kappa_p)={}_{O} \langle k_1, \dots, k_r \rangle$ and let $R \in O^{r \times m}$ be a matrix whose $i$-th row equals $k_i$.
conclusions: the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $ \lbrace p \rbrace$ is given by $$ \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V= \left\lbrace g\in \mathcal{A}_O^m \; | \; R \bullet g=0 \right\rbrace. $$
nodes.statement_short: The VMPUM of one polynomial signal $p$ is the solution set of a matrix whose rows generate $\ker(\kappa_p)$.
nodes.label: vmpum

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: By the definition of $R$ and Remark \ref{ann}, it is clear that $\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace \subseteq \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V $. It remains to show that $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }$ is most powerful. Suppose there exists another behavior $\mathcal{B}'$ unfalsified by $p$. The behavior $\mathcal{B}'$ possesses a kernel representation $R' \in O^{r' \times m}$. By the definition of $R$, there exists a matrix $X \in O^{r' \times r}$ such that $R'=XR$. But since $(X \cdot R) \bullet p = X \bullet (R \bullet p)$, it follows that $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V \subseteq \mathcal{B}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Unfalsified by Remark 2.8; most powerful because any other kernel representation $R'$ factors as $XR$.

nodes.name: Unfalsified
nodes.statement: By the definition of $R$ and Remark \ref{ann}, it is clear that $\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace \subseteq \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V $.
nodes.statement_short: By Remark 2.8, $p$ lies in the model.

nodes.name: Remains: most powerful
nodes.statement: It remains to show that $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }$ is most powerful.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing the model is most powerful.

nodes.name: Other unfalsified behavior
nodes.statement: Suppose there exists another behavior $\mathcal{B}'$ unfalsified by $p$. The behavior $\mathcal{B}'$ possesses a kernel representation $R' \in O^{r' \times m}$. By the definition of $R$, there exists a matrix $X \in O^{r' \times r}$ such that $R'=XR$.
nodes.statement_short: Take another unfalsified behavior; its kernel representation factors through $R$.

nodes.name: Inclusion
nodes.statement: But since $(X \cdot R) \bullet p = X \bullet (R \bullet p)$, it follows that $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V \subseteq \mathcal{B}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the inclusion into the other behavior.

nodes.name: VMPUM of the cuspidal cubic over several Ore algebras
nodes.statement: Let us consider a more interesting example than Example \ref{MotivatingExample} with respect to our favorite algebras from Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}. Let $\Omega=\{\omega\}$ consists of the cuspidal cubic $$\omega(t_1,t_2)=t_1^3-t_2^2.$$ Let us denote by $\mathcal{A}_O=\mathbb{C}[[t_1,t_2]]$ the ring of formal power series and consider the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ $ \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \lbrace f \in \mathcal{A}_O \; | \; R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} \bullet f= 0 \rbrace $ of $\Omega$ with respect to several operator algebras $O$. \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose $O$ to be the second \textbf{Weyl algebra} (see Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}). Then by using {\sc Singular} we obtain: $$ R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \partial_2^3 \\ \partial_1 \partial_2 \\ \partial_1^3 + 3 \partial_2^2 \\ t_2 \partial_2^2-\partial_2 \\ t_2 \partial_1^2 + 3 t_1 \partial_2\\ 2 t_1 \partial_1+3 t_2 \partial_2-6 \end{array} \right]. $$ Now let us determine $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V$ to see how precise the description given by the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ is. Let $f \in \mathcal{A}_O$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\partial_2^3 \bullet f = 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; f=c_0 + c_1 t_2 + c_2 t_2^2, \;$ where $c_i \in \mathbb{C}[[t_1]]$. \item $\partial_1 \partial_2 \bullet f = 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; \partial_1\bullet c_1 + 2 t_2 \partial_1 \bullet c_2=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; \partial_1\bullet c_1 =0 \; \wedge \; \partial_1\bullet c_2 =0$ $ \Rightarrow \;\; c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{C} $. \item $ (\partial_1^3 + 3 \partial_2^2) \bullet f=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; \partial_1^3 \bullet c_0 +6 c_2=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; c_0 = -c_2 t_1^3 + d_2t_1^2 + d_1 t_1 +d_0, \;$ where $ d_i \in \mathbb{C}$. \item $(t_2 \partial_2^2-\partial_2) \bullet f=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; c_1=0 $. \item $(3 t_1 \partial_2+t_2 \partial_1^2) \bullet f=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; d_2=0$. \item $(2 t_1 \partial_1+3 t_2 \partial_2-6) \bullet f = 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; -4d_1t_1-6d_0 = 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\;d_1=0=d_0$. \end{enumerate} Hence, we obtain that $f=c(t_1^3 - t_2^2)$, thus $$ \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \{ c (t_1^3 - t_2^2) \ | \ c\in \mathbb{C} \}.$$ With respect to the requirement of being most powerful and linear, the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ is as significant as possible. We observe that the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of a single non-zero signal has $\mathbb{C}$-dimension one. Actually, this holds in general, as will be shown in Theorem \ref{CDimension}. \item Suppose $O$ to be the second \textbf{difference algebra} see Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}. Then by using {\sc Singular} we obtain: $$R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Delta_2^3\\ \Delta_1 \Delta_2\\ \Delta_1^3+3 \Delta_2^2\\ 2 t_2 \Delta_2^2+\Delta_2^2-2 \Delta_2\\ 2 t_2 \Delta_1^2+\Delta_1^2+6 t_1 \Delta_2+6 \Delta_2\\ 8 \Delta_1^2 +21 \Delta_2^2 + 24 t_1 \Delta_1+36 t_2 \Delta_2-24 \Delta_1-18 \Delta_2-72 \end{array} \right]. $$ Similar arguments as above lead us to $$\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \{ c (t_1^3 - t_2^2) \ | \ c\in \mathbb{C} \}.$$ \item Suppose $O$ to be the second \textbf{$\mathcal{SW}$ algebra} see Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}. Then by using {\sc Singular} we obtain: $$ R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Delta_2^3\\ \Delta_1\Delta_2\\ \Delta_1^3+3\Delta_2^2\\ 2\partial_2+\Delta_2^2-2\Delta_2\\ 2\partial_1+\Delta_1^2-2\Delta_1+2\Delta_2^2\\ 2t_2\Delta_2^2+\Delta_2^2-2\Delta_2\\ 2t_2\Delta_1^2+\Delta_1^2+6t_1\Delta_2+6\Delta_2\\ 8\Delta_1^2+21\Delta_2^2+24t_1\Delta_1+36t_2\Delta_2-24\Delta_1-18\Delta_2-72 \end{array}\right]. $$ Note that generators in the output depend on the monomial ordering of the operators. In this example $\Delta_{1,2}$ were chosen to be greater that $\partial_{1,2}$. Taking a reverse ordering produces different (but equivalent) answer. Comparing this matrix with the matrix above, we see that the rows of the matrix belonging to the difference case appear also here. We conclude that $$\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \{ c (t_1^3 - t_2^2) \ | \ c\in \mathbb{C} \}.$$ Thus, taking $\mathcal{SW}$ as operator algebra, we have got more equations than with the difference algebra. However, we have obtained very interesting mixed differential-difference equations, which show the interplay of two different operator settings. \item The second \textbf{$q$-difference algebra} see Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}: \begin{small} $$ R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \partial_2^2+(-q^2+1) \partial_2\\ (-q-1) \partial_1+(-q^2-q-1) \partial_2+(q^4+q^3-q-1)\\ t_1^3 \partial_2-t_2^2 \partial_2+(q^2-1) t_2^2 \end{array}\right]. $$ \end{small} \begin{enumerate} \item The first equation yields: \begin{align*} &\;\; \sum_{i,j}c_{i,j}(q^j-1)^2t_1^it_2^j + (-q^2+1) \sum_{i,j}c_{i,j}(q^j-1)t_1^it_2^j = 0 \\ \Leftrightarrow & \;\;(q^j-1)^2+(-q^2+1)(q^j-1)=0 \\ \Leftrightarrow & \;\; j=0 \vee j=2. \end{align*} \item Now consider the second equation. \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose $j=2$, then \begin{align*} & \;\;(-q-1)\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(q^i-1)t_1^it_2^2 +(-q^2-q-1) \sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(q^2-1)t_1^it_2^2\\ & \;+(q^4+q^3-q-1)\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}t_1^it_2^2=0\\ \Leftrightarrow & \;\; (-q-1)(q^i-1)+(-q^2-q-1)(q^2-1)+(q^4+q^3-q-1)=0 \\ \Leftrightarrow & \;\; i=0. \end{align*} \item Suppose $j=0$, then \begin{align*} & \;\;(-q-1)\sum_{i,j}c_{i0}(q^i-1)t_1^i +(q^4+q^3-q-1)\sum_{i}c_{i0}t_1^i=0 \\ \Leftrightarrow & \;\; i=3. \end{align*} Thus \quad $f = c_{30} t_1^3 + c_{02}t_2^2$. \end{enumerate} \item Applying the last equation, we get \begin{align*} \;\;t_1^3 c_{02}(q^2-1)t_2^2 -t_2^2 c_{02}(q^1-1)t_2^2 +(q^2-1) t_2^2 ( c_{30} t_1^3 + c_{02}t_2^2 ) =0\\ \Leftrightarrow \;\; t_1^3t_2^2(q^2-1)( c_{30} + c_{02} ) = 0 \;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\; c_{30} =-c_{02}. \end{align*} \end{enumerate} Thus we obtain once more $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \{ c (t_1^3 -t_2^2) \ | \ c\in \mathbb{C} \}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Computes the VMPUM of $t_1^3-t_2^2$ over the Weyl, difference, $\mathcal{SW}$ and $q$-difference algebras; in each case it is the line spanned by the signal.
nodes.label: VMPUMex

nodes.name: Smaller generating sets for the VMPUM
nodes.statement: As we have seen in the previous example, the number of equations giving the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ depends strongly on the underlying Ore algebra. In all cases, with Gr\"obner bases we get more equations than it might be actually necessary. However, it is possible to compute a smaller generating set, which is usually not a Gr\"obner basis. Namely, one computes a left syzygy module of a given system and almost directly deduces a smaller generating set from it. As an example, we show that only 3 of 6 equations from the first example of \ref{VMPUMex} generate the whole ideal, namely $\partial_1 \partial_2, \partial_1^3+3 \partial_2^2, 2 t_1 \partial_1+ 3 t_2 \partial_2-6$. Analogous smaller generating sets can be obtained for other examples.

nodes.name: Kernel representation matrix $R$ for several signals
nodes.statement: A kernel representation of the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega=\{\omega_1, \dots, \omega_N \}$ is determined by stacking a set of generators of $$\bigcap_{i=1}^N \ker( \kappa_{\omega_i} )$$ row-wise into a matrix $R$.

nodes.name: VMPUM of a finite set of signals
nodes.statement: Using the notation from above, the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$ equals $$\mathcal{B}_{\Omega}^V= \left\lbrace g \in \mathcal{A}_O^m \; | \; R \bullet g=0 \right\rbrace.$$
assumptions: Using the notation from above
conclusions: the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$ equals $$\mathcal{B}_{\Omega}^V= \left\lbrace g \in \mathcal{A}_O^m \; | \; R \bullet g=0 \right\rbrace.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: By the definition of $R$, it is clear that $\Omega \subseteq \mathcal{B}_\Omega^V$. Also the property of being most powerful follows by the same arguments as used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{vmpum}.
nodes.statement_short: Same argument as for Theorem 4.2.

nodes.name: VMPUM of $\{t, v_0t-v_1t^2\}$ over the first Weyl algebra
nodes.statement: Suppose $O$ to be the first Weyl algebra and $\mathcal{A}_O=\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$. Consider the signal set $\Omega = \{ t, v_0 t-v_1 t^2\}$, where $v_0, v_1 \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$. The second trajectory will appear in Example $\ref{wurf}$ again. Since \begin{align*} & \ker(\kappa_t) \cap \ker(\kappa_{v_0t-v_1t^2})\\ & = {}_{\mathrm{W}_1} \langle t \partial-1,\ \partial^2 \rangle \cap {}_{\mathrm{W}_1} \langle -v_0^2 \partial^2+(4v_1^2 t- 2v_0v_1)\partial-8v_1^2 ,\ \partial^3 \rangle \\ & = {}_{\mathrm{W}_1} \langle t^2 \partial^2 - 2 t \partial + 2 , \partial^3 \rangle, \end{align*} the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$ is given by $ \mathcal{B}_\Omega^V=\{ c_1 t + c_2 t^2 \ | \ c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{C} \}$. The intersection of submodules of a free module over a Noetherian Ore algebra can be computed as in Corollary \ref{corBasics}, for instance with the system \textsc{Singular::Plural} \cite{Plural}.

nodes.name: $n$-th Weyl algebra $\mathrm{W}_n$
nodes.statement: In this section, we suppose $O$ to be the $n$-th Weyl algebra \begin{center} $O = \mathrm{W}_n:= \mathbb{C}[t_1, \dots, t_n][ \partial_1; \mathrm{id}_{ \mathrm{W}_n}, \frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}] \cdots [ \partial_n; \mathrm{id}_{ \mathrm{W}_n}, \frac{\partial}{\partial t_n}].$ \end{center} Thus for $p \in\mathbb{C}[t_1, \dots, t_n]$, we obtain $ \partial_i \bullet p := \frac{\partial p}{\partial t_i}$.
nodes.section: 5 VMPUM by using the polynomial Weyl algebra

nodes.name: Smooth function signal space
nodes.statement: Further suppose $\mathcal{A}_O $ to be $\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{C})$, the space of smooth functions. Identifying a polynomial with the corresponding polynomial function, we obtain $A \subseteq \mathcal{A}_O$.
nodes.section: 5 VMPUM by using the polynomial Weyl algebra

nodes.name: VMPUM is finite-dimensional
nodes.statement: A known result is that the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over~$\mathbb{C}$, since it is contained in the corresponding $\mathrm{MPUM}$ \cite{VMPUM}.
conclusions: the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over~$\mathbb{C}$

nodes.name: Exponent sets $\mathcal{E}_i$ and degrees $d_{ij}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{E}_i:=\left\lbrace \beta_{i1}, \dots, \beta_{ih_i} \right\rbrace \subset \mathbb{N}_0^n$ denote the set of all exponent multi-indices occurring in $p_i$ and let \begin{eqnarray} d_{ij}:=\max_{1\leq k \leq h_i} \left\lbrace (\beta_{ik})_j \; | \; \beta_{ik} \in \mathcal{E}_i \right\rbrace \end{eqnarray} be the highest degree in $t_j$ of $p_i$.

nodes.name: Highest degree $d_{ij}$
nodes.statement: d_{ij}:=\max_{1\leq k \leq h_i} \left\lbrace (\beta_{ik})_j \; | \; \beta_{ik} \in \mathcal{E}_i \right\rbrace
nodes.label: expo

nodes.name: Index set $\mathcal{E}_{p_i}$
nodes.statement: The set $$ \mathcal{E}_{p_i}=\{ \alpha \in {\mathbb{N}}_0^n \, | \, \alpha_j \leq d_{ij}+1 \; \mbox{ for } \, 1\leq j \leq n \} $$ is finite, that is, $\mathcal{E}_{p_i} = \lbrace \alpha_{i1}, \dots, \alpha_{il_i} \rbrace$.

nodes.name: Derivative set $\mathrm{Der}_p$
nodes.statement: Define for $p\in A^m$ $$ \mathrm{Der}_p=\lbrace p_1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{11}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{11}}}, \dots,\frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{1l_1}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{1l_1}}}, \, \dots \, , p_m, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{m1}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{m1}}}, \, \dots \,, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{ml_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{ml_m}}} \rbrace.$$

nodes.name: Polynomial syzygy module $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$ denote the module of polynomial syzygies.

nodes.name: Homomorphism $\Phi_p$
nodes.statement: Define for the matrix $M=[ 1 e_1, \; \partial^{\alpha_{11}} e_1, \; \dots, \; \partial^{\alpha_{1l_1}}e_1, \; \dots, \; 1 e_m, \; \partial^{\alpha_{m1}}e_m, \; \dots, \; \partial^{\alpha_{ml_m}} e_m]^T$ the $A$-module homomorphism $$\Phi_p:\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p) \rightarrow \ker(\kappa_p), \;\;\; (q_1, \dots, q_l) \mapsto (q_1, \dots, q_l) \cdot M, $$ which is clearly injective.
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi_p$ maps a polynomial syzygy of $\mathrm{Der}_p$ to an operator in $\ker(\kappa_p)$ by multiplying with the matrix $M$ of monomial derivatives.

nodes.name: $\ker(\kappa_p)$ is generated by the image of $\Phi_p$
nodes.statement: ${}_{\mathrm{W}_n}\langle \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p) \rangle = \ker(\kappa_p)$.
conclusions: ${}_{\mathrm{W}_n}\langle \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p) \rangle = \ker(\kappa_p)$.
nodes.label: KomCom

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: Evidently ${}_{\mathrm{W}_n} \langle \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p) \rangle \subseteq \ker(\kappa_p)$. Now suppose that $a \in \ker(\kappa_p)$. Since every element in $\mathrm{W}_n$ can be written in normal form, we obtain \begin{align*} a \bullet p & = \sum_k a_k \bullet p_k = \sum_k ( \sum_j c_{kj} t^{\beta_{kj}} \partial^{\gamma_{kj}} ) \bullet p_k \\ & = \sum_k ( \sum_j c_{kj} t^{\beta_{kj}})( \partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k ). \end{align*} Let us split the element $a$ in $a_z$ and $a_{nz}$ such that $a=a_z+a_{nz}$ and $(a_z)_k$ consists of the parts of $a_k$ where $\partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k$ is zero. By the choice of $d_{ij}$, the set $\{ \partial_j^{(d_{ij} +1)} \, | \, 1\leq j \leq n, \; 1 \leq i \leq m \}$ generates the set of $\partial^\gamma$ with the property that there exists $1 \leq i \leq m$ such that $ \partial^\gamma \bullet p_i=0.$ Then $a_z$ is contained ${}_{W_n}\langle \partial^{(d_{ij} +1)e_j} \, | \, 1\leq j \leq n, \; 1 \leq i \leq m \rangle$. But by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, the element $a_z$ is in the image of $\Phi_p$. Suppose $\partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k \neq 0$, then $\gamma_{kj}$ is equal or smaller than $(d_{k1}, \dots, d_{kn})$ in each component and again by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, the element $a_{nz}$ is contained in the image of $\Phi_p$. Thus it follows that $a \in \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Split an operator in $\ker(\kappa_p)$ into the part killing $p$ termwise and the rest; both lie in the image of $\Phi_p$ by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$.

nodes.name: Easy inclusion
nodes.statement: Evidently ${}_{\mathrm{W}_n} \langle \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p) \rangle \subseteq \ker(\kappa_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: The image of $\Phi_p$ lies in the kernel.

nodes.name: Expand $a\bullet p$ in normal form
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $a \in \ker(\kappa_p)$. Since every element in $\mathrm{W}_n$ can be written in normal form, we obtain \begin{align*} a \bullet p & = \sum_k a_k \bullet p_k = \sum_k ( \sum_j c_{kj} t^{\beta_{kj}} \partial^{\gamma_{kj}} ) \bullet p_k \\ & = \sum_k ( \sum_j c_{kj} t^{\beta_{kj}})( \partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k ). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Take $a$ in the kernel and expand its action in normal form.

nodes.name: Split $a=a_z+a_{nz}$; $a_z$ in the image
nodes.statement: Let us split the element $a$ in $a_z$ and $a_{nz}$ such that $a=a_z+a_{nz}$ and $(a_z)_k$ consists of the parts of $a_k$ where $\partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k$ is zero. By the choice of $d_{ij}$, the set $\{ \partial_j^{(d_{ij} +1)} \, | \, 1\leq j \leq n, \; 1 \leq i \leq m \}$ generates the set of $\partial^\gamma$ with the property that there exists $1 \leq i \leq m$ such that $ \partial^\gamma \bullet p_i=0.$ Then $a_z$ is contained ${}_{W_n}\langle \partial^{(d_{ij} +1)e_j} \, | \, 1\leq j \leq n, \; 1 \leq i \leq m \rangle$. But by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, the element $a_z$ is in the image of $\Phi_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $a$ into terms whose derivatives of $p$ vanish and the rest; pure derivatives killing $p_i$ are generated by $\partial_j^{d_{ij}+1}$, so $a_z$ is in the image.

nodes.name: $a_{nz}$ in the image
nodes.statement: Suppose $\partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k \neq 0$, then $\gamma_{kj}$ is equal or smaller than $(d_{k1}, \dots, d_{kn})$ in each component and again by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, the element $a_{nz}$ is contained in the image of $\Phi_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining derivatives are bounded by the degrees, hence covered by $\mathrm{Der}_p$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus it follows that $a \in \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $a$ lies in the image.

nodes.name: VMPUM of a single nonzero signal is one-dimensional
nodes.statement: The $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $p \neq 0$ is a one-dimensional vector space over~$\mathbb{C}$.
assumptions: $p \neq 0$
conclusions: The $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $p \neq 0$ is a one-dimensional vector space over~$\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.label: CDimension

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.2
nodes.statement: We use the notation of the Lemma \ref{KomCom}, which reduces to commutative calculations. It is easy to see that the equivalence \begin{align} s \bullet (f_1, \partial^{\alpha_{11}} \bullet f_1, \dots, f_m, \dots, \partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet f_m)^T = 0 \;\;\;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\;\;\; \Phi_p(s) \bullet f =0 \end{align} holds for every $ s \in \mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p) $. Now let us discuss the left hand side. More precisely, let us consider the solution space $\mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p))$ in $\mathcal{A}_O$ belonging to $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$. Since $\mathrm{Der}_p$ contains all non-zero derivatives of $p_i$ for all $i$, there exists a non-zero constant ${\mathbb{C}} \ni k \in \mathrm{Der}_p$. We can suppose $k=1$ and without loss of generality let $\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet p_m=1$. Then $$(-1, 0, \dots, 0, p_1), \; \dots, \; (0, \dots, 0, -1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \in \mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$$ and thus \begin{align} \mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)) = \lbrace c \cdot (p_1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{11}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{11}}}, \dots, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \; | \; c \in {\mathbb{C}} \rbrace. \end{align} Now suppose $f \in \mathrm{VMPUM}_p$. From Lemma \ref{KomCom} together with (\ref{SolDModCom}) and (\ref{SolCom}) we deduce the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via Lemma 5.1 to the commutative syzygy system of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, whose solution space is one-dimensional because $\mathrm{Der}_p$ contains a nonzero constant.

nodes.name: Reduce to commutative computation
nodes.statement: We use the notation of the Lemma \ref{KomCom}, which reduces to commutative calculations.
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma 5.1 to reduce to commutative calculations.

nodes.name: Equivalence of solution conditions
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that the equivalence \begin{align} s \bullet (f_1, \partial^{\alpha_{11}} \bullet f_1, \dots, f_m, \dots, \partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet f_m)^T = 0 \;\;\;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\;\;\; \Phi_p(s) \bullet f =0 \end{align} holds for every $ s \in \mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p) $.
nodes.statement_short: Relate solutions of a syzygy to solutions of its image under $\Phi_p$.

nodes.name: Solution space of the syzygies
nodes.statement: Now let us discuss the left hand side. More precisely, let us consider the solution space $\mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p))$ in $\mathcal{A}_O$ belonging to $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Consider the solution space of $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$.

nodes.name: Nonzero constant in $\mathrm{Der}_p$
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{Der}_p$ contains all non-zero derivatives of $p_i$ for all $i$, there exists a non-zero constant ${\mathbb{C}} \ni k \in \mathrm{Der}_p$. We can suppose $k=1$ and without loss of generality let $\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet p_m=1$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Der}_p$ contains a nonzero constant; normalise it to 1.

nodes.name: Compute $\mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p))$
nodes.statement: Then $$(-1, 0, \dots, 0, p_1), \; \dots, \; (0, \dots, 0, -1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \in \mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$$ and thus \begin{align} \mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)) = \lbrace c \cdot (p_1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{11}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{11}}}, \dots, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \; | \; c \in {\mathbb{C}} \rbrace. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit syzygies force the solution space to be the line through the derivative vector.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Now suppose $f \in \mathrm{VMPUM}_p$. From Lemma \ref{KomCom} together with (\ref{SolDModCom}) and (\ref{SolCom}) we deduce the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 5.1 with the two displays.

nodes.name: Syzygy solutions versus $\Phi_p$ solutions
nodes.statement: s \bullet (f_1, \partial^{\alpha_{11}} \bullet f_1, \dots, f_m, \dots, \partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet f_m)^T = 0 \;\;\;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\;\;\; \Phi_p(s) \bullet f =0
nodes.label: SolDModCom

nodes.name: Solution space of $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$
nodes.statement: \mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)) = \lbrace c \cdot (p_1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{11}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{11}}}, \dots, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \; | \; c \in {\mathbb{C}} \rbrace.
nodes.label: SolCom

nodes.name: VMPUM is the most precise linear description
nodes.statement: In the case of a single non-zero signal, the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ gives the most precise description one can get for a linear system.

nodes.name: MPUM and VMPUM of $v_0t-v_1t^2$
nodes.statement: Consider the trajectory $\omega(t)=v_0 t - v_1 t^2$, where $v_0,v_1\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\{0\}$. Then the $\mathrm{MPUM}$ of $\omega$ is given by \begin{align*} \mathcal{B}_{\{\omega\}} &= \{ \alpha (v_0t-v_1t^2)+\beta(v_0-2v_1t)+ \gamma (-2v_1) \ | \ \alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{R} \} \\ & = \{ at^2 + bt +c \ | \ a, b, c \in \mathbb{R} \}\\ & = \{ w \in \mathcal{A}_O \ | \ \partial^3 \bullet w = 0 \}. \end{align*} Thus there are three free parameters to choose. The $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\omega$ is given by \begin{align*} \mathcal{B}^V_{\{ \omega\}} & =\{ w \in \mathcal{A}_O \ | \ \left[ \begin{array}{c} -v_0^2 \partial^2+(4v_1^2 t- 2v_0v_1)\partial-8v_1^2 \\ \partial^3 \end{array} \right] \bullet w = 0 \} \\ & = \{ c \, ( v_0 t - v_1 t^2 ) \ | \ c \in \mathbb{R} \}, \end{align*} that is, two degrees of freedom vanish when we consider the time-variant model.
nodes.statement_short: For the trajectory $v_0t-v_1t^2$ the MPUM has three free parameters while the VMPUM has one.
nodes.label: wurf

nodes.name: Degree on $\mathrm{W}_n$
nodes.statement: Since every element of $\mathrm{W}_n$ can be transformed into normal form, the degree of an element $a\in\mathrm{W}_n$ can be introduced as $$ \deg(a):= \max \lbrace \; \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i + \beta_i \;\; | \;\; a = \sum_{\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{N}_0^n} a_{\alpha, \beta} t^{\alpha} \partial^{\beta}, \; a_{\alpha, \beta} \in \mathbb{C} \rbrace. $$

nodes.name: Bernstein filtration
nodes.statement: Then $\mathcal{F}^i(\mathrm{W}_n):=\left\lbrace a \in \mathrm{W}_n \; | \; \deg(a)\leq i \right\rbrace $ induces a filtration on $\mathrm{W}_n$.

nodes.name: Associated graded ring of $\mathrm{W}_n$
nodes.statement: The corresponding associated graded ring $\mathrm{Gr}(\mathrm{W}_n)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}[t_1, \dots, t_n, \!\partial_1, \dots, \partial_n]$ as a graded $\mathbb{C}$-algebra.

nodes.name: Hilbert polynomial of a $\mathrm{W}_n$-module
nodes.statement: For every finitely generated $\mathrm{W}_n$-module $M$, we define the Hilbert polynomial $\mathrm{HP}_M^{\mathrm{W}_n}:=\mathrm{HP}_{\mathrm{Gr}(M)}^{\mathrm{Gr}(\mathrm{W}_n)}$.

nodes.name: Dimension of a $\mathrm{W}_n$-module
nodes.statement: The dimension of $M$ is defined as $\dim_{\mathrm{W}_n}(M):=\deg(\mathrm{HP}_M)+1.$

nodes.name: Holonomic module
nodes.statement: Furthermore $M$ is called \textbf{holonomic} if it has dimension $n$.

nodes.name: Holonomic modules have minimal dimension
nodes.statement: A holonomic module is of minimal dimension, since the dimension of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules is bounded below by $n$ and bounded above by $2n$.
conclusions: A holonomic module is of minimal dimension
the dimension of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules is bounded below by $n$ and bounded above by $2n$

nodes.name: Holonomic modules are cyclic and torsion
nodes.statement: Holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules are additionally cyclic and torsion modules.
conclusions: Holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules are additionally cyclic and torsion modules.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m}/\ker(\kappa_p)\cong A$ is simple holonomic
nodes.statement: There is an isomorphism of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong A.$ In particular, $\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p)$ is simple holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-module.
conclusions: There is an isomorphism of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong A.$
$\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p)$ is simple holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-module.
nodes.label: WeylCAlgebra

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.5
nodes.statement: Since $\kappa_p$ is a homomorphism of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules, we get $$ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong \mathrm{Im}(\kappa_p) \subseteq \mathrm{W}_n / {}_{\mathrm{W}_n} \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_n \rangle \cong A. $$ Thus $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) $ is isomorphic to a submodule of $A$. Due to the fact that $A$ is a simple holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-module and $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \neq 0$ the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: The quotient embeds into $\mathrm{W}_n/\langle\partial\rangle\cong A$, which is simple holonomic, and is nonzero.

nodes.name: Embed into $A$
nodes.statement: Since $\kappa_p$ is a homomorphism of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules, we get $$ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong \mathrm{Im}(\kappa_p) \subseteq \mathrm{W}_n / {}_{\mathrm{W}_n} \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_n \rangle \cong A. $$
nodes.statement_short: First isomorphism theorem and Theorem 2.7 embed the quotient into $A$.

nodes.name: Submodule of $A$
nodes.statement: Thus $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) $ is isomorphic to a submodule of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: The quotient is a submodule of $A$.

nodes.name: Simplicity of $A$
nodes.statement: Due to the fact that $A$ is a simple holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-module and $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \neq 0$ the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero submodule of the simple module $A$ is $A$.

nodes.name: Cyclic presentation $\mathrm{W}_n/L_p$
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p)$ is holonomic, there exists a left ideal $L_p$, depending on $p$, such that $\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) $ is isomorphic to the cyclic left $\mathrm{W}_n$-module $\mathrm{W}_n / L_p $.
assumptions: Since $\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p)$ is holonomic

nodes.name: Discrete shift criterion for pairwise different exponents
nodes.statement: Now consider \begin{align} p = \left[ \begin{array}{c} p_1 \exp_{\lambda^{(1)}} \\ \vdots \\ p_m \exp_{\lambda^{(m)}} \end{array}\right] , \;\; \mbox{ where } \; \lambda^{(i)} \in K^n \setminus \left\lbrace 0\right\rbrace, \; \mbox{ and } \; p_i \in A \end{align} and suppose $\lambda^{(1)}, \dots, \lambda^{(m)}$ to be pairwise different and without loss of generality $\lambda^{(i)}_j \neq 0$ for all $1 \leq i \leq m$ and $1\leq j\leq n$. Then \begin{align} \sum_{j=1}^m a_j \bullet (p_j \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}}) =0 \;\;\; \mbox{if and only if}\;\;\;[a_1, \dots, a_m] \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m \chi_{\lambda^{(j)}}(\,\ker(\kappa_{p_j}) \,), \end{align} which follows by $$\sum_{j=1}^m a_j \bullet (p_j \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}}) = 0 \; \Leftrightarrow \; \sum_{j=1}^m \left( \sum_{i=1}^{h_j} c_{ji} t^{\alpha_{ji}} \Delta^{\beta_{ji}} \bullet (p_j \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}})\right) = 0 $$ $$\Leftrightarrow \sum_{j=1}^m (\chi_{\lambda^{(j)}}^{-1}(a_j) \bullet p_j) \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}} =0 \Leftrightarrow \chi_{\lambda^{(j)}}^{-1}(a_j) \, \in \, \ker(\kappa_{p_j}) \;\; \mbox{ for all } \, 1 \leq j \leq m.$$

nodes.name: VMPUM of polynomial-exponential signals (difference algebra)
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be of the form (\ref{shiftexpvektor}). Further let $K_i:= \left\lbrace j \; | \; \lambda^j= \lambda^i \right\rbrace = \left\lbrace k_{i1}, \dots, k_{i l_i}\right\rbrace $ and $l$ chosen minimal such that the disjoint union $K_1 \dot \cup \dots \dot \cup K_l = \left\lbrace k_{11}, \dots, k_{1h_1}, \dots, k_{l1}, \dots, k_{lh_l} \right\rbrace =\left\lbrace 1, \dots, m \right\rbrace $. Further define the vector $h_i:=[f_{k_{i1}}, \dots, f_{k_{il_i}}]^{T}$ and $H_i:=\chi_{\lambda^{(i)}}( \ker(\kappa_{h_i}) )$. Let $e_{k_{ij}}$ denote the $k_{ij}$-th standard generator of $\mathcal{S}_n^{1 \times m}$ for $1\leq i \leq l$ and $1 \leq l \leq h_i$. Defining for $1 \leq i \leq l$ \begin{align*} \phi_i: H_i \rightarrow \mathcal{S}_n , \;\;\; [a_1, \dots, a_{h_i}] \mapsto \sum_{j=1}^{h_i} a_j e_{k_{ij}} \end{align*} the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $p$ is given by $ \;\;\bigoplus_{i=1}^l \phi_i(H_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Discrete analogue of Theorem 5.8: the VMPUM is the direct sum of $\chi_{\lambda^{(i)}}$-shifted kernels for each group of equal exponents.

nodes.name: Dimension of the VMPUM of independent signals
nodes.statement: Let $p=[p_1, \dots, p_m]$ consist of $\mathbb{C}$-linear independent signals. We conjecture that $\dim_\mathbb{C}(\mathrm{VMPUM}(p))=m$.
assumptions: Let $p=[p_1, \dots, p_m]$ consist of $\mathbb{C}$-linear independent signals.
conclusions: $\dim_\mathbb{C}(\mathrm{VMPUM}(p))=m$
